opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important distinction, and people often conflate the two. The fundamental approach is something like the core idea — the thing you could write on a napkin. "Train a big transformer on next-token prediction." "Do RL on verifiable rewards." "Have the model think out loud before answering." Those ideas are often surprisingly simple, and in hindsight they seem almost obvious. A lot of the time, the basic idea has been floating around in the literature for years before it actually works.

Then there's this enormous iceberg underneath: the details needed to make it work. Which data mixture, how you normalize, the learning rate schedule, how you keep the RL from collapsing or reward hacking, how you get the infrastructure to run stably across thousands of GPUs. That stuff is where most of the engineering effort and tacit knowledge goes. It's often the difference between "this idea doesn't work" and "this idea is a paradigm shift."

The way I'd distinguish them is roughly: the fundamental approach is what determines the scaling trajectory — what you get if you keep pouring compute into it. The details determine whether you're on that curve at all, and with what constant factor. Details matter enormously for who wins in the short run, but the fundamental approach tells you where the whole field is going.

And this has real implications for security, which is something I care a lot about. People sometimes say, "Oh, the ideas are all public anyway, what's the secret?" But the key algorithmic secrets often aren't the napkin idea — they're the details. If an adversary gets the napkin idea, they still have to spend a year rediscovering all the tricks. If they get the details, they can just skip ahead. So the details are, in some sense, where a lot of the lead actually lives.

r001.rationale: It contrasts simple core ideas that fit on a napkin with the many data, training, and infrastructure details needed to make them work.

r002.rationale: It says these ideas are often surprisingly simple and seem almost obvious in hindsight.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really important distinction, and it's one that people outside the labs often get wrong. There's the sort of high-level idea, the paradigm, and then there's the enormous amount of engineering grind that it takes to actually make the idea work at scale.

Take something like RLHF, or more recently the whole RL-on-reasoning thing. The core idea, you could write it on a napkin. Train a reward model, do policy optimization against it, or just do RL on verifiable outcomes with chain of thought. People had basically proposed versions of these ideas years before they worked. And so if you just look at the napkin, you'd say, well, this is obvious, anyone could do it.

But that's not the hard part. The hard part is the thousand details. How do you keep the thing from reward hacking? How do you deal with the fact that your training becomes unstable at some scale and you have no idea why for three weeks? What's the data mix, what's the learning rate schedule, how do you handle the infrastructure so you're not burning half your compute on idle GPUs? And each of those individually seems small, but you stack a hundred of them and that's the difference between a thing that works and a thing that doesn't.

The way I'd put it is: the fundamental approach is what tells you where to dig. The details are the actual digging. And the thing that's interesting is that the approach is usually not secret, or not secret for long. Someone publishes a paper, or you hear a rumor, or honestly you can infer it from how the model behaves. The details are the secret sauce. That's what the labs are actually protecting. That's where the thousands of person-years of effort are.

And I think this matters a lot for how you think about things like algorithmic progress and the gaps between labs and, frankly, security. Because if you think the key is the big idea, you think, okay, once that leaks, the game is over. But actually, you can know the big idea and still be a year or two behind, because you haven't done the grind. Conversely, if someone gets the actual details, the code, the hyperparameters, the hard-won lessons about what breaks, that's a much bigger deal than people appreciate. That compresses the timeline enormously.

One more thing I'd say is that it's not always clean which bucket something falls into. Sometimes what looks like a detail turns out to be the whole thing. Like, the insight that you need to scale a certain way, or that some normalization trick is what unlocks training at a certain size. Was that a fundamental approach or a detail? Kind of both. The people who've done it enough times develop a sense for which details are load-bearing, and that taste is maybe the real scarce resource.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a high-level idea that can be written on a napkin with the many engineering details required to make it work at scale.

r002.rationale: It says the idea can look obvious in retrospect and that versions of these approaches had been proposed years before they worked.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish the core idea from the recipe. The core idea might be something you can explain in a few sentences: here’s the objective, here’s why this should let the model learn something it couldn’t learn before. But that doesn’t mean you can take those sentences and reproduce the result.

The recipe is all the things you discover by actually running experiments. What data do you use? How do you make training stable? How do you know whether an experiment failed because the idea is wrong or because you chose the wrong hyperparameters? Those details can represent an enormous amount of work.

And the distinction isn’t perfectly clean. Sometimes the thing that looks like an implementation detail is precisely what makes the approach work at scale. So you can have the right fundamental idea and still be quite far from having a working system.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a core idea that can be explained in a few sentences with the experimental recipe and implementation details needed to reproduce a working system.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that a successful training solution may seem obvious in retrospect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two levels. There’s the basic idea, which you can often explain in a couple of sentences, and then there’s figuring out how to actually make it work at scale. And the second part can contain an enormous amount of intellectual work. You have to get the data right, get the optimization stable, figure out which experiments are informative, and understand why something that worked in a small run stops working in a large one.

So calling those things “details” can be misleading. The fundamental approach tells you where to look. It doesn’t necessarily give you a recipe. You could tell two teams the same basic idea, and one might spend six months getting nowhere while the other produces a major advance, because they’ve accumulated the experimental judgment to make it work.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an idea explainable in a couple of sentences with the extensive data, optimization, and experimentation work needed to make it succeed at scale.

r002.rationale: The response discusses execution difficulty and experimental judgment but does not suggest that a successful solution seems obvious in retrospect.
